question.leadin: Answer some questions about the history of the Netherlands, whose name literally means "low-lying countries"
question.text: Part of the modern-day Netherlands gained independence from the Spanish Empire in a war named for this many years, which is how long it lasted.

swap.leadin: Give the following about Belgian involvement in World War II.
swap.text: After the surrender of Belgium in 1940, the Belgian government evacuated from this capital city to form a government-in-exile in London.
swap.clue: This northern European capital city is sometimes called "The Capital of Europe" because it serves as the de facto capital of the European Union.

question.leadin: This woman, born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle, was known as Agent H-21 to French intelligence.
question.text: Name this dancer who was executed in 1917 for spying for Germany.
question.clue: This person adopted a Malay name that meant "eye of the day" as a stage name.

swap.text: In 1637 the Dutch economy was harmed by the sudden price collapse of these flowers whose species include Bokhara and Viceroy.
swap.clue: Beginning in the Netherlands during the Dutch Golden Age, forty of these flowers sold for 100,000 guilders.

question.leadin: This country had a colony at Tianjin in China.
question.text: Name this country whose capital is Brussels. This country's other colonial ventures included a stint in Guatemala and as co-ruler of the Moroccan Tangier International Zone.
question.answerHtml: Kingdom of Belgium [accept Koninkrijk België, accept Royaume de Belgique, accept Königreich Belgien]
question.clue: The 2008 financial crisis affected this nation's banks Fortis and Dexia, and occurred under the Prime Ministership of Yves Leterme and Herman van Rompuy .

swap.text: This Flemish geographer created a 1569 world map that represented sailing courses as straight lines and distorted Greenland to the size of Africa.
swap.clue: This University of Leuven scholar, who created a 1569 world map, led the "golden age of Netherlandish cartography." This engraver, who coined the term "atlas," names a widely-used but controversial map "projection."

question.leadin: A rejected 1937 law in this country was derisively nicknamed the Maulkuerfgesetz, or the "muzzle law," and sought to outlaw the Communist Party.
question.text: Name this "Gibraltar of the North" which helps to name a European zone with Belgium and the Netherlands.
question.clue: Known as the Gibraltar of the North, this nation's fortifications were improved upon by Vauban under Louis XIV.

swap.text: The Treaty of Munster ended the Eighty Years' War and gave this nation independence. This country allied with Sweden during the war and was led by Maurice and Frederick Henry.
swap.clue: A force from this country was defeated in a siege by a man who was born to a member of the Tagawa family and would go on to become the first ruler of the Kingdom of Tungning.

question.text: Napoleon III denied a Hohenzollern prince with this name the chance to ascend to the Spanish throne, precipitating the Franco-Prussian War. A man with this name was crowned king of a new country after an 1830 revolution that broke out at an opera performance.
question.clue: Atrocities committed under a king of this name were detailed in the Casement Report which included accounts of his Force Publique severing the limbs of workers who failed to meet rubber quotas.

swap.leadin: Identify the following about the violent history of Europe.
swap.text: Organized by the Duke of Alba, this court in the Spanish Netherlands attempted to suppress Calvinism and tighten Spanish control over the Netherlands by enforcing the Tenth Penny tax.
swap.answerHtml: Council of Blood [or Council of Troubles; or Raad Van Beroerten; or Bloedraad; or Tribunal de los Revoltosos; or Tribunal de Sangre; accept reasonable equivalents for "Council", such as "Court" ]
swap.clue: This tribunal created by the Duke of Alba to deal with unrest in the early stages of the Dutch Revolt.

question.text: This son of William the Silent was a stadtholder and an important strategist during the Dutch revolt. This protege of Oldenbarnevelt successfully besieged Breda.
question.clue: This man used the alleged crime of raising of waargelder forces as an excuse to execute his the pro-Arminianism and pro-peace rival Johan van Oldenbarnevelt.

swap.leadin: According to the book The Bookshop of the World, during this period, 10 times more books were produced per capita than in France or Spain.
swap.text: Name this period, also the subject of Simon Schama's The Embarrassment of Riches. This period's end is traditionally dated to the "Disaster Year" of 1672.
swap.answerHtml: Dutch Golden Age [or Gouden Eeuw; or Netherlands Golden Age; or Dutch Miracle; prompt on Golden Age]

question.leadin: Name these people associated with Dutch exploration of the land down under.
question.text: On two expeditions, this explorer in the employ of the Dutch East India Company discovered Tonga, Fiji, New Zealand, and an island now named for him, which is separated from Australia by the Bass Strait.
question.clue: His companions included the merchant Isaac Gilsemans, whose drawings depict their travels, and the carpenter Frans Visscher, who planted flags for him in the name of Prince Frederick Hendrick.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the rise and fall of Johan van Oldenbarnevelt ("olden-BAR-nuh-velt").
swap.text: This lawyer was tried alongside van Oldenbarnevelt for expressing tolerance toward the Arminians. This author of the international law book Mare Liberum escaped Loevestein ("LOO-vuh-stain") Castle while hidden in a book chest.
swap.answerHtml: Hugo Grotius [or Huig de Groot or Hugo de Groot]
swap.clue: This Dutch thinker and author of On the Laws of War and Peace is considered one of the founders of International Law.

question.text: This Dutch Admiral active during the Franco- and Anglo-Dutch wars commanded at the Four Days' and St. James's Day battles before destroying the docked British fleet in the daring Raid on the Medway.
question.clue: He became friends with Frederick III of Denmark after relieving a Swedish siege of Danzig without fighting.

swap.leadin: This event began when attendees of Daniel Auber's opera La Muette de Portici joined Catholic rioters outside the theater doors after hearing the duet "Sacred Love of the Fatherland."
swap.text: Name this 1830 event led by Charles Rogier ("roh-zhee-AY"). The Ten Days' Campaign supported by William I failed to topple a monarch installed during this event.
swap.answerHtml: Belgian Revolution [or Révolution Belge; or Belgische Revolutie; or Belgische Opstand; or Belgische Omwenteling; prompt on Belgian independence]
swap.clue: Sparked by perceived anti-Catholic policies, it brought to power the widower of Princess Charlotte of Wales, who later arranged the marriage of his niece Victoria to his nephew Albert.

question.leadin: The RAF and US Army Air Forces attempted to alleviate this event by organizing food drops termed Operation Manna and Operation Chowhound.
question.text: Name this massive famine that took place in German-occupied Netherlands at the end of World War II.

swap.text: This great Dutch admiral defeated the Spanish under Antonio de Oquendo at the Battle of the Downs, a key win for the Dutch during the Eighty Years War. He clashed with Robert Blake during the First Anglo-Dutch War, in which he died.

question.text: Homo Ludens and In the Shadow of Tomorrow are other works of this early 20th century Dutch historian best known for The Waning of the Middle Ages.
question.clue: This historian, who wrote how the 15th century "inculcated the idea of death in the collective mind" in The Autumn of the Middle Ages.

swap.leadin: In the eighteenth century, emphasis placed on clinical practice and physiology led this city to surpass Padua as a center of medical learning.
swap.text: Name this city where modern medical instruction was pioneered by Herman Boerhaave. This institution's famed Hortus Botanicus was located next to an observatory built to house Rudolph Snellius's great quadrant.
swap.clue: This city celebrates Thanksgiving due to its brief role as safe harbor for the pilgrims who boarded the Mayflower, though they did so because English thugs came here to brutally assault William Brewster. It's home to a university founded in 1575 that hosted Justus Lipsius and Franciscus Gomarus.
